text.en: The Olympic Games are older than Rome: the first were held in 776 BC, and by tradition the city was founded only 23 years later.
Around 880 BC, Lapita seafarers landed on Tonga — at nearly the same time the Phoenicians founded Carthage. Two great ages of seafaring, worlds apart.
The fire that destroyed Nineveh in 612 BC baked the clay tablets of Ashurbanipal's library — helping them survive to the present day.
The terracotta sculptures of Nigeria's Nok culture were being made centuries before China's Terracotta Army of Qin Shi Huang.
By traditional dating, the Buddha, Confucius and Pythagoras were contemporaries: all three lived in the 6th century BC.
Confucius died in 479 BC — one year after the Greeks defeated the Persian fleet at Salamis.
Rome expelled its last king in 509 BC and Athens got democracy from Cleisthenes in 508: republic and democracy were born almost side by side.
India's Maurya Empire arose about a year after Alexander the Great died — and its founder, Chandragupta, is said to have met Alexander himself.
Almost simultaneously, Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BC) and repented the bloodshed, while China saw the Battle of Changping (260 BC), one of antiquity's bloodiest.
In 202 BC, empires were decided at both ends of Eurasia: Scipio defeated Hannibal at Zama, and Liu Bang founded the Han dynasty.
Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes measured the Earth's circumference in Egypt, while Chinese chroniclers made the first sure record of Halley's Comet.
The earliest known Long Count calendar date in Mesoamerica is 36 BC — just five years before the Battle of Actium.
The first Olympic champion on record was a cook. Coroebus of Elis, a cook and baker, won the only event held in 776 BC: a single sprint of one stadion.

Women could not compete at Olympia, yet in 396 BC the Spartan princess Cynisca became an Olympic champion. In chariot racing the prize went to the owner of the horses, not the driver, and she won it twice.
Carthage is older than Rome. By the traditional dates the Phoenicians founded it in 814 BC, 61 years before Romulus founded Rome. In 146 BC the younger city would destroy the older one.
Yerevan is 29 years older than Rome. The city traces itself to the Urartian fortress of Erebuni, founded in 782 BC, a date known not from legend but from King Argishti I's own cuneiform inscription.
The oracle did not lie to Croesus: a great empire did fall, his own. Herodotus says Delphi told the Lydian king that if he attacked Cyrus he would destroy a great empire. He attacked, and lost Lydia.

The idiom 'the writing on the wall' comes from the fall of Babylon. In the Book of Daniel a hand writes 'mene, mene, tekel, upharsin' on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, and that very night the king is slain.

The Hanging Gardens of Babylon may not have been in Babylon at all. Oxford scholar Stephanie Dalley argues the legend describes the Assyrian king Sennacherib's gardens at Nineveh, over 400 km north, later credited to Nebuchadnezzar.

The tale that Phoenicians sailed around Africa c. 600 BC is believable thanks to a detail Herodotus rejected: Pharaoh Necho II's sailors said the Sun was on their right. That is exactly what you see sailing west south of the equator.

Herodotus wrote that in India gold was dug up by ants bigger than foxes. Explorer Michel Peissel offered an answer: on Pakistan's Deosai Plateau marmots bring gold dust up from their burrows, and 'ant' may be a mistranslation from Persian.

The word 'magic' is Persian in origin. The magi were priests of Media and Persia, already named in Darius's Behistun inscription around 520 BC. Greeks saw them as sorcerers and astrologers, hence 'magician' and 'magic'.
Persia was met at Thermopylae not by 300 Spartans but by some 7,000 Greeks, about 300 of them Spartans. Hundreds of Thespians and Thebans also stayed with Leonidas to the end.

A well by the Acropolis held 190 potsherds bearing Themistocles' name, written in just 14 hands. They seem to have been prepared to hand out to voters at an ostracism, more like modern how-to-vote cards than outright fraud.
One of history's shortest replies came from Sparta. Philip II warned: 'If I invade Laconia, I shall turn you out.' The ephors answered with one word: 'If.' Laconia gave us the word 'laconic'.
Sparta, tradition says, banned gold and silver coins and used heavy iron money instead. Xenophon explained that wealth became too bulky to hide. The law was credited to the semi-legendary Lycurgus.

Socrates' last words were about a rooster he owed. After drinking the hemlock he said: 'Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?' Asclepius, god of healing, was given a cock in thanks for a cure.

Pythagoras is said to have forbidden his followers to eat fava beans. Later biographers even claimed he talked a bull out of eating beans and made a bear swear never to harm a living thing, and that the bear kept its word.

Legend says a Pythagorean was drowned for discovering irrational numbers. The sect held that everything is a ratio of whole numbers, and Hippasus supposedly proved otherwise. Yet no ancient writer actually credits him with the discovery.
Diogenes did not live in a barrel but in a pithos, a huge clay storage jar, in Athens. When a youth broke it, the Athenians gave the philosopher a new one.

Tradition holds that the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus burned on the very day Alexander the Great was born. Plutarch quipped that the goddess failed to save it because she was busy delivering Alexander.
The word 'mausoleum' is a man's name. Mausolus was a Persian satrap of Caria, and his tomb at Halicarnassus, now Bodrum, was one of the Seven Wonders. Ever since, any grand tomb has been a mausoleum.

French phare and Italian and Spanish faro are all the name of one Egyptian island. Pharos, off Alexandria, gave its name to the lighthouse that stood on it, and that lighthouse to lighthouses in many languages.

The Library of Alexandria grew by confiscation. Galen says that under Ptolemy II every book found on ships entering the port was seized and copied; the owners got the copies and the library kept the originals.

An Egyptian king kept the original scripts of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides and simply forfeited a huge deposit. Ptolemy III borrowed them from Athens against 15 talents, had luxury copies made, sent those back and kept the originals.

The word 'geography' was coined by the first man to measure the Earth. Eratosthenes, chief librarian at Alexandria, introduced the terms 'geography' and 'geographer', and was also first to calculate the tilt of Earth's axis.
The Romans did not sow Carthage with salt. No ancient source says so: the salt story appears in books only from the 19th century and was probably modelled on the Biblical tale of Shechem.

After destroying Carthage, the Roman Senate paid to translate one Punic book: Mago's 28 volumes on farming. The city's libraries went to Numidian kings, but Mago's manual was brought to Rome and rendered into Latin.
SPQR, 'the Senate and People of Rome', still appears on Rome's coat of arms and city documents. Italians jokingly expand it as Sono Pazzi Questi Romani: 'These Romans are crazy.'

Augustus did not steal a day from February to make his month as long as July. Sextilis was renamed for him in 8 BC and already had 31 days. The stolen-day story was invented by the 13th-century scholar Johannes de Sacrobosco.
Roman soldiers were not paid in salt. Latin salarium, the root of 'salary', is linked to salt somehow, but no ancient source says troops received salt as pay, or even a salt allowance.

A one-eyed queen of Kush fought Rome and won a good peace from Augustus. Strabo says Amanirenas was blind in one eye; her troops took Syene and Elephantine, and after talks Augustus imposed no tribute on Kush.

The principle behind the camera was first described by the Chinese philosopher Mozi around 400 BC: light passing through a pinhole into a dark room paints an upside-down image. This is the camera obscura.

More than 100,000 of Confucius's descendants lie in his family cemetery at Qufu. Over two and a half millennia the Kong family graveyard has grown to 183 hectares and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

China's First Emperor sought immortality and may have been poisoned by it: one theory blames a mercury elixir from his alchemists. The soil of his tomb mound holds 100 times the natural mercury, as Sima Qian wrote of rivers of mercury inside.

The Amazons may not be pure myth. Many graves of armed Scythian and Sarmatian women warriors have been found across the Eurasian steppe, likely the inspiration for the Greek legend; one turned up near Voronezh in 2019.

Gleaming white Greek statues and temples were originally painted in bright colours. The paint had weathered off long before the 18th century, so Europe fell for bare marble the ancients never saw. Traces of paint survive on the Parthenon too.

The tattoos of the 'Ukok Princess' are some 2,400 years old. The mummy of a 5th-century BC Pazyryk woman was found in 1993 in an ice-filled Altai kurgan, with deer still visible on her shoulder and wrist.

The first Olympic Games and the fall of China's Western Zhou are five years apart: the games traditionally date to 776 BC, and in 771 BC nomads sacked the Zhou capital, opening the Spring and Autumn period.

Chinese history has exact years earlier than Greek history. The first securely dated year in Sima Qian's records is 841 BC — 65 years before the first Olympiad, which the Greeks later used to count time.
In 356 BC Alexander the Great was born, and the state of Qin began Shang Yang's reforms. Alexander's empire fell apart the moment he died; Shang Yang's reforms led Qin to unify China 135 years later.
As the Greeks faced Persia at Marathon, the Zapotecs in Mexico were levelling a mountaintop to build a capital on it. Monte Albán was founded around 500 BC and lasted more than a thousand years.
The world's oldest pile carpet is a contemporary of Socrates. Woven around the 5th century BC, it survived in the permafrost of an Altai burial mound and is now in the Hermitage.

Hannibal took elephants over the Alps at almost the same time China began its Great Wall. Carthage crossed the mountains in 218 BC; China, unified in 221 BC, started linking old walls into one a few years later.

Legend says Persia conquered Egypt with the help of cats. Polyaenus wrote that at Pelusium in 525 BC Cambyses placed animals sacred to the Egyptians in front of his army, and the Egyptians would not shoot.
When a cat died in an Egyptian house, everyone in it shaved off their eyebrows, Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BC. Diodorus claimed that killing a cat, even by accident, could get you lynched.
Alexander’s men marvelled at an Indian reed that “yields honey without bees”. That was how his admiral Nearchus described sugarcane in 326 BC, a plant Europe barely knew.
“Rich as Croesus” refers to the king who first struck coins of pure gold and pure silver. Before him Lydia minted electrum, a natural alloy whose value was hard to check.
The word “salary” is often said to come from Roman soldiers being paid in salt. But Roman sources do not confirm any such payment; it is most likely a pretty folk etymology.
Alexander the Great named a city after his horse. When his faithful Bucephalus died in India in 326 BC, the king founded the city of Bucephala on the banks of the Hydaspes.
The ancient Greek 'computer' had a dial for the Olympics. One of the Antikythera mechanism's scales tracked the four-year cycle of the Panhellenic games, a calendar of the great sporting events.
Cleopatra was not Egyptian: her Ptolemaic dynasty was Macedonian Greek. According to Plutarch she was the first of her line, in more than 250 years, to learn the Egyptian language.
Julius Caesar was almost certainly not born by caesarean section. In Rome the operation was performed only on dead or dying mothers, and his mother Aurelia lived some 46 more years after his birth.

Legend says Confucius once went to Laozi for advice. The historian Sima Qian writes that the young Confucius asked the Zhou archivist about ritual and afterwards likened him to a dragon beyond understanding.
